# The Department of Unfinished Things

On her first morning at the Department of Unfinished Things, Mara was given a brass key, a chipped blue mug, and a warning not to complete anything without written authorization.

“Not even a sentence?” she asked.

Her supervisor, Mr. Vale, looked up from his desk.

“Especially a sentence.”

The department occupied the fourth floor of a municipal building that appeared, from the street, to have only three. Visitors reached it by pressing the elevator button marked with a small scratch. Most people never noticed the scratch. Those who did generally assumed it was damage and looked away, embarrassed on behalf of the city.

Mara had found the job advertisement inside a library book.

**CLERK REQUIRED. Must tolerate ambiguity. Pension available.**

At the time, ambiguity seemed preferable to unemployment.

Mr. Vale led her through a room of tall cabinets. Each drawer bore a handwritten label: APOLOGIES, DOMESTIC PROJECTS, EDUCATIONS, JOURNEYS. One entire wall was devoted to NOVELS. Somewhere inside it, a typewriter struck a single key every few minutes.

“What exactly do we do?” Mara asked.

“We preserve what people leave unfinished.”

“Why?”

“Because it has to go somewhere.”

He opened a drawer marked CONVERSATIONS: INTERRUPTED BY WEATHER. Inside lay hundreds of little glass cylinders, each holding what looked like a breath on a cold morning.

He lifted one.

“‘I’ve been meaning to tell you,’” he read from its tag. “‘November fourteenth. Railway platform. Hail.’”

“What was the person going to say?”

“That isn’t our business.”

He returned the cylinder gently.

At her desk, Mara found a ledger, a fountain pen, and a tray containing her first assignment: a half-knitted green sock.

The attached form listed its owner as Mrs. Anika Bell, eighty-three, deceased.

“Do we give it to her family?”

“Not unless they request it.”

“Couldn’t someone finish knitting it?”

Mr. Vale rested both hands on the back of her chair.

“Possibly. But a finished sock would be a sock. At present it is also a Tuesday afternoon, a radio playing in another room, and a woman expecting to have more time.”

He left her with that.

Mara entered the sock’s details in the ledger.

Under CONDITION, she wrote: Good.

After a moment, she crossed it out.

She wrote: Unfinished.

The morning passed quietly. At noon, someone wheeled a trolley between the desks. It carried sandwiches, tea, and a jigsaw puzzle showing a lighthouse. Three pieces were missing.

“Is that department property?” Mara asked.

“No,” said the woman pushing the trolley. “It’s just annoying.”

Her name was Iona. She had worked there twenty-six years.

Over lunch, she explained the practical rules. Do not shake an unfinished argument. Do not read a love letter aloud. If a drawer smells of seawater, call Maintenance.

“And don’t let Vale frighten you,” she said. “He only sounds like that because he’s been here so long.”

“How long?”

Iona considered.

“I’ve never asked.”

***

By October, Mara could distinguish an abandoned ambition from a postponed one by weight.

Abandoned ambitions were surprisingly light. Postponed ones could strain your wrist.

She learned to file half-learned languages in padded envelopes because loose words escaped at night. She learned that unfinished chess games continued developing grudges. She learned that the cabinet of interrupted dances required oiling every Friday, though it contained no machinery.

Most arrivals came through the intake hatch behind her desk.

A scarf.

A dissertation.

A father’s attempt to explain the divorce.

Each arrived accompanied by a form in the same neat handwriting, though nobody knew who completed the forms.

Mara became good at her work.

She had always been good at arranging things. After her mother died, she had sorted the kitchen cupboards by expiration date. After her fiancé left, she had alphabetized the books they had bought together, removing his and closing the gaps.

There was comfort in making one thing follow another.

Every evening, she returned to her flat, cooked something sufficient, and opened the drawer beneath the telephone.

Inside lay a postcard addressed to her brother.

Dear Daniel,

She had written those two words four years earlier.

They had not quarreled dramatically. There had been no slammed door, no unforgivable speech. Instead, during their mother’s illness, a thousand small disagreements had accumulated until ordinary conversation required a kind of strength neither possessed.

Daniel thought Mara had made decisions without consulting him.

Mara thought Daniel had mistaken asking questions for helping.

Both could produce evidence.

After the funeral, he moved north. They exchanged birthday messages for a while. Then they stopped.

The postcard showed a seaside town they had visited as children. On its front, a gull stood on a railing, looking severely disappointed in the ocean.

Each evening Mara looked at Dear Daniel.

Each evening she closed the drawer.

At work, she began noticing how many objects arrived in pairs that never met: a question in one cabinet, an answer three rooms away; a marriage proposal beside a refusal written six months earlier.

“Do we ever reunite them?” she asked Iona.

“Sometimes.”

“How?”

“Usually by accident. Deliberate reunions need three signatures.”

“And accidental ones?”

“A different form.”

In November, the department received a bridge.

It appeared in the intake hatch at eleven seventeen, although the hatch was no larger than a bread box.

For a moment, Mara saw stone arches stretching into mist. Then the bridge folded itself into a space the size of a shoebox and settled on her desk.

Its form read: MUNICIPAL FOOTBRIDGE, EAST BRANCH. CONSTRUCTION SUSPENDED, 1936.

“What happened?” she asked.

“Funding,” said Mr. Vale.

He studied the little arches with an expression she had not seen before.

“Where was it meant to lead?”

“To the other side.”

But when Mara glanced at him, she thought he had nearly said something else.

***

The trouble began with a memo.

It arrived on thick paper bearing the city seal and the phrase OPERATIONAL EFFICIENCY REVIEW.

An inspector would visit the department on Monday.

“Is that bad?” Mara asked.

Iona put down her tea.

“The last review merged Lost Causes with Public Complaints. Nobody slept properly for a month.”

Mr. Vale read the memo twice. Then he locked it in his desk.

The inspector arrived carrying nothing but a slim gray folder.

Her name was Ms. Crisp. She wore shoes that made no sound and greeted everyone with the professional warmth of a person confirming an appointment.

“I’m here to understand your outcomes,” she said.

Mr. Vale showed her the cabinets.

Ms. Crisp took notes.

“And how many items do you process each year?”

He told her.

“How many do you resolve?”

“We don’t generally resolve them.”

“Then what does processing mean?”

“Cataloguing. Stabilizing. Preservation.”

“For what eventual purpose?”

Mr. Vale looked toward the long room.

“Availability.”

Ms. Crisp wrote something down.

She spent the morning examining drawers. She asked whether the unfinished symphonies could be completed by the unfinished composers. She suggested selling unfinished houses as development opportunities. She wanted to know why the department retained New Year’s resolutions older than seven years.

At lunch, she declined a sandwich.

By three, she had reached her conclusion.

“The inventory is growing without limit. Your storage model is unsustainable.”

“People keep living,” Iona said.

“Yes,” said Ms. Crisp. “That has been identified as a contributing factor.”

Her proposal was simple.

The department would conduct a general clearance. Items would either be returned to their owners for prompt completion or designated permanently abandoned and destroyed.

“You can’t require people to finish things,” Mara said.

“Of course not. There will be an opt-out box.”

“And if they don’t answer?”

“Nonresponse will constitute abandonment.”

From the wall of novels came the sound of a thousand pages turning at once.

Mr. Vale stood.

“This department exists because a thing may matter without ever being finished.”

Ms. Crisp closed her folder.

“I appreciate that this is an emotional workplace.”

After she left, nobody spoke for a while.

Then Iona said, “Well. We’d better put the kettle on.”

The clearance notices went out that Friday.

By Monday, the city had become strange.

A retired dentist began building the boat he had sketched at nineteen. He laid the keel across his driveway, blocking his wife’s car.

Two former friends met in a café to resume an argument about a borrowed coat.

A woman walked into a university lecture thirty-one years late.

At first, the newspapers called it a renaissance.

Then the complaints started.

People stayed awake trying to remember why they had wanted what they once wanted. Elderly men climbed ladders. Old resentments arrived at doorsteps carrying flowers.

The department’s intake hatch rattled day and night.

For every thing completed, several new things remained undone.

***

Mara found Mr. Vale in the bridge cabinet.

He had placed the little bridge on a table. Mist drifted beneath its arches.

“There was supposed to be a garden on the far bank,” he said.

Mara sat beside him.

“My wife drew the plans. Chestnuts along the path. Benches facing west.”

“Was she an architect?”

“No. A person with opinions about benches.”

He smiled briefly.

“They stopped construction in winter. By spring she was ill.”

Mara looked at the bridge.

“Is that why you work here?”

“I came to inquire about it. They needed someone temporarily.”

“How long ago?”

“Long enough that temporarily has become misleading.”

From the next room came a muffled crash. An unfinished renovation was reacting badly to its clearance notice.

“Can we stop this?” Mara asked.

“Crisp has authority.”

“Who gave it to her?”

“The city.”

“Could we ask the city to take it back?”

“Certainly. There’s an appeals process.”

“How long?”

“Nine to fourteen months.”

The first destruction was scheduled for Thursday.

That evening, Mara opened the drawer beneath her telephone.

The postcard was gone.

In its place lay a clearance notice.

**ITEM: CORRESPONDENCE, SIBLING.**

**STATUS: PENDING DETERMINATION.**

She sat down hard.

At the bottom of the page were two boxes.

COMPLETE.

ABANDON.

For several minutes she stared at them.

Then she turned the notice over and wrote: Neither.

At work the next morning, she gave it to Ms. Crisp, who had installed herself in the conference room.

“That isn’t an available category,” the inspector said.

“It should be.”

“You’ve had four years.”

“I know.”

“How much longer do you need?”

“I don’t know.”

Ms. Crisp tapped the paper against the table.

“There must be a point at which indecision becomes a decision.”

“Maybe. But I can’t tell you the date.”

The inspector looked tired.

For the first time, Mara noticed that the gray folder’s corners were worn soft.

“What have you left unfinished?” she asked.

“That isn’t relevant.”

“Nothing?”

Ms. Crisp said nothing.

Somewhere beyond the wall, the typewriter struck its lonely key.

Finally, she opened the folder.

Inside was a photograph of a room with bare plaster walls. Sunlight fell across an upright piano.

“My daughter wanted me to learn with her,” she said. “One piece. Four hands.”

“What happened?”

“She grew up.”

“Where is she now?”

“Not far.”

Mara waited.

“I thought,” Ms. Crisp said, and stopped.

The intake hatch opened in the next room.

Both women heard it.

Ms. Crisp shut her folder.

“No,” Mara said gently. “You can finish that sentence here.”

The inspector looked at her for a long time.

“I thought there would be an ordinary evening when we could begin.”

Mara glanced at the photograph again. There was a second stool beside the piano, barely visible at its edge.

***

They did not save the department with a speech.

They saved it with paperwork.

Ms. Crisp discovered an obscure provision allowing inventory to be reclassified as civic infrastructure if it served an ongoing public function.

Bridges qualified.

So did reservoirs.

After some discussion, and one exceptionally long lunch, she agreed that certain unfinished things might be described as reservoirs.

Of possibility, Mr. Vale suggested.

“Don’t put that in the official version,” she said. “Put deferred utility.”

The revised proposal established three categories: active, resting, and released.

Owners could request their unfinished things back. They could leave them in safekeeping. They could also let them go, without pretending they had never mattered.

Nothing would be destroyed for failure to answer a letter.

It was not perfect.

There were budget reductions. Two cabinets had to share a drawer. Journeys lost its window.

But Thursday came and went without the furnaces being lit.

On Friday, Iona brought a cake.

The icing read: PROVISIONALLY APPROVED.

Mara took her postcard home.

For three nights, she left it on the kitchen table. On the fourth, she put it in a larger envelope and added a sheet of paper.

Dear Daniel,

I keep trying to find a fair account of what happened, and I don’t think I can. I was angry with you. I expect you were angry with me. Some days I still am, which makes this awkward.

I saw this postcard and remembered you stealing chips from the gulls, which remains the most foolish contest I have ever witnessed.

Would you like to have lunch sometime?

She read it once before she could reorganize it into silence.

Then she posted it.

Daniel replied nine days later.

His letter was short.

He remembered the gulls differently. He had been defending the chips.

Lunch would be good.

They met halfway between their homes, in a town neither knew. The restaurant was too warm, and Daniel had grown a beard Mara disliked immediately.

For twenty minutes they discussed trains.

Then he asked about her work.

“It’s difficult to explain,” she said.

He nodded.

He had always hated it when she said that. She remembered, and began again.

“I look after things people haven’t finished.”

“Like what?”

“Socks. Books. Bridges.”

“Bridges?”

“Occasionally.”

He waited for her to smile. When she didn’t, he tore a piece from his bread roll and considered this.

Outside, a bus struggled around a corner.

Mara wanted to ask whether he had been lonely. She wanted to explain the hospital forms, the calls she had made, the last morning. Instead she asked whether he wanted coffee.

“Yes,” he said. “I’m not in a hurry.”

Back at the department, the postcard’s ledger entry had changed.

Not to complete.

Not to resolved.

In Mr. Vale’s careful handwriting, it said:

**Returned to use.**
